Quarto and Pandoc keep a good deal of state about a render: which format is being written, which file is being read, which version is running, what the reader and writer options are.
All of it is reachable from a Lua filter, and none of it from the document you are writing.

`lua-env` copies that state into the document's metadata.
Once it has run, a value from the render environment can be printed with a shortcode, the same way any other metadata is, and optionally written out as JSON.

## Installation

```bash
quarto add {{< var extension.reference >}}
```

This will install the extension under the `_extensions` subdirectory.
If you are using version control, you will want to check in this directory.

Or install it from your editor with [Quarto Wizard](https://m.canouil.dev/quarto-wizard):

::: {.btn-group role="group" aria-label="Quarto Wizard installer options"}

[Visual Studio Code](vscode://mcanouil.quarto-wizard/install?repo={{< var extension.wizard-reference >}}){.btn .btn-outline-primary title="Install {{< var extension.reference >}} in Visual Studio Code using the Quarto Wizard extension."}

## Quick start

The filter has to be enabled before the shortcode has anything to read:

```yaml
filters:
  - path: lua-env
    at: pre-quarto
```

Then name a value by its dot-separated path:

```markdown
{{{< lua-env pandoc.FORMAT >}}}
```

This page renders to {{< lua-env pandoc.FORMAT >}}, under Pandoc {{< lua-env pandoc.PANDOC_VERSION >}}.

The same values are reachable through Quarto's own `meta` shortcode, under the `lua-env` key:

```markdown
{{{< meta lua-env.pandoc.FORMAT >}}}
```

See the [Reference](reference.qmd) for every option and every path, and the [Examples](examples.qmd) for values printed live.

## Where it works

Every output format.
The values differ by format, which is rather the point: `pandoc.FORMAT` is `html` here and `latex` in a PDF.
